You use instances of the type to access data of a specific type in memory.
You are responsible for handling the life cycle of any memory you work with through unsafe pointers to avoid leaks or undefined behavior.
You use the type to access and manage memory that has been bound to a specific type.

Many pointer operations must only be applied to pointers with memory in a specific state—you must keep track of the state of the memory you are working with and understand the changes to that state that different operations perform.
Uninitialized memory must be initialized before it can be accessed for reading.
When you access memory through an instance, the type must be consistent with the bound type of the memory.

Strings always have value semantics.
Comparing strings for equality using the equal-to operator ( ) or a relational operator (like or ) is always performed using Unicode canonical representation.

Basic string operations are not sensitive to locale settings, ensuring that string comparisons and other operations always have a single, stable result, allowing strings to be used as keys in instances and for other purposes.
If you need to access the contents of a string as encoded in different Unicode encodings, use one of the string’s , , or properties.

To find individual elements of a string, use the appropriate view for your task.
